summary: Charles Frye from Modal Labs addresses the AI Engineer World's Fair on benchmarking LLM inference engines for open-weights models. He notes open models (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek) have caught up to proprietary ones for many production use cases, validating his 2023 prediction that open collaborative projects dominate once capability requirements saturate, analogous to operating systems and databases. Three main open-source engines are benchmarked: vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. Modal built a public benchmark at modal.com/llm-almanac covering approximately 10 models, 3 engines, and ~10 context lengths using out-of-box unoptimized configurations, with executable code snippets and downloadable raw data for reproducibility. Live demonstrations show Qwen 3 MoE and Gemma 3 27B each achieving ~1 req/sec on vLLM for generation-heavy workloads (128 in, 1024 out), while RAG workloads (1024 in, 128 out) achieve ~4 req/sec—a 4x improvement driven by parallel prefill's arithmetic-intensive matrix-matrix multiplications versus autoregressive decode's memory-bound pattern. Crucially, first-token latency remains nearly identical despite 10x more input tokens, making context augmentation 'basically a free lunch.' Frye advises product teams to reach for context rather than reasoning when improving quality, as it is cheaper and easier to meet latency SLOs. He notes BF16 lacks fast tensor core support compared to FP8/FP4 on Hopper and Blackwell, where multiplication speedup is quadratic in bit width, so FP4 on Blackwell would widen the gap further. Benchmarking methodology exposes maximum parallelism (1000 concurrent requests) for peak throughput and sequential single requests for minimum latency, sweeping between these extremes. Per-replica throughput is measured on a single H100; total throughput scales out by adding replicas, not scaling up. Common SLOs include 1-second first-token latency for general use and 300ms for interactive applications.

sections.title: Open Models Catch Up to Proprietary
sections.summary: Frye introduces the shift from proprietary-model dominance to viable open-weights self-hosting, driven by Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek model series and matured software stacks with optimizations like KV caching, paged attention, multi-token prediction, and speculative decoding. He names vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM as the key open-source inference engines.

sections.title: Revisiting 2023 Predictions
sections.summary: Frye recaps his 2023 AI Engineer Summit talk predicting that if capability requirements saturate, open collaborative projects will catch up and dominate, analogous to operating systems and databases. He notes TGI is gone while vLLM persisted, and claims three of his 2023 slides were correct.

sections.title: Building the LLM Almanac Benchmark
sections.summary: Modal built a public benchmark at modal.com/llm-almanac covering ~10 models across vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM at ~10 context lengths, motivated by customer questions about self-hosting performance. Configurations use out-of-box performance without optimization, with community contributions encouraged especially for TensorRT-LLM.

sections.title: Live Benchmark Demonstrations
sections.summary: Live demos show Qwen 3 MoE (~1 req/sec on vLLM, 128 in/1024 out) and Gemma 3 27B (similar throughput, vLLM outperforming SGLang). A key finding emerges: RAG workloads (1024 in, 128 out) achieve ~4 req/sec versus ~1 req/sec for generation-heavy workloads, illustrating the throughput advantage of parallel prefill over autoregressive decode.

sections.title: Analysis, Advice, and Methodology
sections.summary: Frye explains the 4x throughput gap: prefill is arithmetic-intensive (large matrix-matrix multiplications) while decode is memory-bound. BF16 lacks fast tensor core support versus FP8/FP4 on Hopper and Blackwell, where speedup is quadratic in bit width, so FP4 on Blackwell would widen the gap further. First-token latency is nearly identical despite 10x more input tokens—a 'free lunch.' He advises reaching for context over reasoning to improve quality cheaply. He describes the benchmarking methodology: send 1000 concurrent requests for peak throughput, send one at a time for minimum latency, and sweep between. Per-replica throughput is on a single H100; total throughput scales out by adding replicas. Raw data is downloadable and benchmark code is open source.

limitations: All benchmarks use out-of-box unoptimized configurations, not carefully tuned

TensorRT-LLM has many opaque tuning knobs (e.g., 'user buffer') that are not well documented
Gemma 3 27B BF16 was the only quant initially working; 8-bit quant was eventually added
BF16 benchmarks do not exercise fast tensor core support available with FP8/FP4 on Hopper and Blackwell
Community contributions needed for optimized implementations and missing configurations
